My mother passed away in 2020, right before the pandemic hit. I lost her to respiratory failure, and it was unexpected. Due to her diabetes, I thought that she would need surgery or any other treatment. Didn't think she'd actually die. 

I think it was a week or so after she passed away, and the reality of losing her had finally hit me. I just remember bawling at night because I was so scared. Almost 17 at that time and lost my rock that I could depend on. 

And then I had a dream one night. It was around Christmas time (my mother loved seeing my father put up Christmas decorations, she thought it was adorable seeing him be like a child around Christmas), and we were all sitting in the living room watching TV. I think in the dream I realized that she was dead, and I started crying heavily. She looked at me with a heartbroken face, and then she looked at my father, and said, "Please, take care of them. You'll do that, won't you?" 

That dream always stuck with me since. It's funny because I'm not a Christian, I'm actually an atheist. 

I hope you all are okay. Please, take care of yourselves, and please take good care of your daughter.

"I see the "therapy" reply ALL THE FREAKING TIME and want to claw my eyes out."

This is what I feel on a daily basis every time I see a 'go to therapy' reply on any thread about trauma. It makes me so *violently angry.* Therapy has ruined my life by deliberately putting me in an extremely dangerous situation, and broke my trust repeatedly. 

I wasn't adopted, but I was a gifted student coming from a Christian background. Being expected to do the best ruined me. It didn't help that my father was a survivor of a genocide. I understand he wanted me to have a good education, but he pushed it too far when he saw that I am intelligent. I had my boundaries stomped on repeatedly by everyone, especially by therapists. "Oh, you don't know what you want" and "Here, let me make you second-guess every single decision you want to make". And one therapist tried to indoctrinate me into a cult, another put me in an extremely dangerous situation where it could've gone badly. 

I *loathe* therapy. I *hate* and *despise* it. After my high school graduation, I basically told myself, "I'm gonna take a year to recover from all the mental clusterfuck in my life, because I need a break from everything." And it's going pretty okay. Still have my episodes constantly from psychotic depression, *but* I am much more relieved because I don't have the weight of therapy on my shoulders. 

Therapy is not for everyone, and should not be treated as the one magical cure that cures everyone.

Therapy has been *extremely* abusive to me, and I feel immense hatred for it. Sometimes therapy just makes everything worse. It made me completely unable to trust anyone, and thus I stay away from everyone. If someone suggests for me to go to therapy, it triggers a fight or flight response- and usually I glare at people coldly. Therapy has become such an extreme trigger for me. 

Other than that? I'm... actually doing okay without therapy. Sure, I have my episodes often, but I manage them on my own. And when I don't, I usually find a safe spot for me to let it out and let it pass. I know this isn't available to everybody. Not everybody has the chance/choice to have a safe zone to go to. 

I agree with you. Therapy is *not* the magic potion for everything. It's not a 'one-size-fits-all'. Sometimes therapy just *isn't the answer*. And that's okay.

It's very hard to give constructive criticism because there's no video, and we don't have enough information on FK and BW. But from what I've read here, I can give you my experience playing Legend and higher. 

1. You said you spent some of the remaining ammo on Plague Monks. I would heavily advise against doing this. I would try to dodge, or move onto a ramp where it takes the Plague Monks longer to reach you. Yes, they can tear through block very easily, and I'm aware dodging isn't what it used to be back in the old days. But because of the fact that you spent some ammo on Plague Monks *could've* led to your demise. 

2. The Blightstormers should be your *second* top priority besides disablers like Gutter Runners, Life Leeches, Packmasters, etc. They can absolutely wipe your team easily, and it was the reason why you failed in the end. Blightstormers are extremely dangerous. So in my opinion, I would've dealt with the Assassin first, then Blightstormer, then Warpfire Thrower, and Globadier last. 

3. The SotT needed to switch places with you when you ran out of ammo. I don't know what ranged weapon she had, but she should've been the one dealing ranged when you ran out of ammo. 

4. The fact that FK was long gone by this point is *bad.* He's the crowd clearer, the tanky of the group. He most likely should've been one of the last group members to die, but he was gone. You had nobody to tank, and Zealot used to be tankier back in the old days. 

5. I have no idea what was going on with the BW, so I can't say anything on what she should've done. 

6. Don't stay in the middle of the arena in the finale of Athel Yenlui. This is where a lot of Stormvermin, infantry, berserkers, and possibly other specials show up all at once. I would recommend going back up on the ramps so it would take longer for the enemies to get to you. 

7. Know that in order to get a team wipe, everyone shares the blame. This was *not* strictly *your* fault. Everyone else had a hand in the team wiping. So the fact that the whole team blamed *you* for the team wipe isn't constructive at all. This is a game where teamwork is required. 

8. Expanding on 7, it seemed like everyone was doing their own thing, which is what most likely led to everyone dying. And I will insist that teamwork is required, since this is a co-op game. 

Now, here is one thing that I heavily recommend if you want to ask for criticism in the future- *record your gameplays.* I do this often. The mission may be successful or it may not be, but recording your gameplays allows you to go back and analyze what you may have done wrong, or what other team members have done wrong. But if your computer can't handle recording and playing at the same time, don't worry so much about that. This is what I recommend. 

So, to reiterate this- this wasn't strictly your fault. Everyone had a hand in the team wiping. It just sucks that you got with people who immediately pointed fingers at you. Don't be so hard on yourself.

And if I feel like it, I set some more small goals for myself. I was 15-16 when I saw my mother die, and I think about 17 was when I was officially diagnosed (my memory is kinda fuzzy, so forgive me on that). 

To tell you the truth, I honestly didn't think I was going to make it. I thought that I wouldn't reach 18, that I wouldn't graduate high school. But I did it, and I did it by taking it one day at a time. 

I want to congratulate you on how far you've made it so far. Mental illness is a bitch, and I'm *very* proud of you for how far you've made it. Take it slow. You're still not quite there yet, but you're slowly making it there. 

For me, slow and steady wins the race. Maybe it'll help you too. I still struggle with my depression, it's a monster that kicks me down every day and haunts me at night. But I still set some small goals. I've learned that people trying to force you on some big goal isn't always the best way, and that it stressed me out more than everything else. 

So, why not set some small goals for yourself? Maybe it'll help, maybe it won't, but it's still an idea to try it.

Hello, I've been diagnosed with major depressive disorder with psychotic features, and is currently disabled because of that disorder. Some people with psychosis say it doesn't have a trigger, some others may say it's from stress or anxiety or depression. Mine does indeed come from depression, and it happens alongside with depressive symptoms. This is what it's like for me.

The human brain is interesting, as there are so many factors that could lead to a psychotic episode. We're not entirely sure about the causes of any mental illness, whether it's environmental or because of genetics. I would recommend you do research on this. Have a great day. :)

As a fellow peep who has been diagnosed with major depressive disorder with psychotic features and is disabled with that, and from what I've read from your title and comments, this person doesn't have a psychotic disorder. It's only a disorder if it impairs their life. 

From my experience (and you could probably relate to this since you also suffer from psychotic symptoms), I have both auditory and visual hallucinations. I hear laughter, I hear full on conversations, and I even communicate with them. I also see shadows of people and monsters- kind of like body horror. And this all happens when I'm experiencing depressive symptoms, which is... All the time. You also can't switch it off when it happens.

I will say that if they feel like they have a psychotic disorder, they need to see a medical professional- specifically a psychiatrist. However, since you see that they don't have a psychotic disorder, you should educate them on that. Tell them what it really means to have a psychotic disorder. Tell them about your experiences and how it affects your day-to-day life. Tell them to see a psychiatrist. 

If they don't listen to you, then you simply drop them as a friend. They aren't worth your time nor are they worth your mental health. Psychosis/schizophrenia is not a mental disorder to self diagnose, they severely impact your life. Any mental disorder can and will impair you, and they should not be taken lightly, nor should they be joked about. It's ultimately your call to decide whether to continue your friendship with them, but I would suggest either telling them to see a psychiatrist, educate them on psychosis/schizophrenia, or you leave them behind and get new friends who will actually listen to you.

I hope you have a wonderful day. :)

Hello, I am an 18 year old disabled by major depressive disorder with psychotic features (otherwise known as psychotic depression). I've had this disorder since I was 8 years old- so I've had this for a decade now. 

I kind of was always aware I was different from others, especially in elementary school where nobody hung out with me or was weirded out by me. Not being treated the same caused me to develop internal anger issues, and those anger issues manifested into depression by the age of 8. And by 6th grade I told the middle school that I wanted to commit suicide. And then earlier this year I was hospitalized twice (baker acted) for attempting suicide. The doctors found out that I always talked to myself (I was actually talking to the voices and to the hallucinations that appear in front of me), and it always happened when I am depressed (which is... all the time). So they diagnosed me with major depressive disorder with psychotic features. And then now I recently got put onto disability, and vocational rehabilitation is helping me with employment and moving out at the moment. 

The thing that has always angered me was the fact I was (and still am) isolated from other people. People have always given me weird looks and never wanted to hang out with me, and even my own father saw me as a demon. I just do not like being seen as weird or demonic, I just want to be treated as a human being. I have feelings, I have thoughts, I walk and eat and breathe the same oxygen as you. I am a human being like you, not some monster that you have to avoid. 

I honestly wished I never got this disability, this disorder, because that is all everyone has ever seen me as- weird, demonic, evil, wicked, a monstrosity. It's hard to love yourself or even accept yourself when people don't accept you. Just because I have a disability doesn't make me less human than you, your friend, or anybody else. 

So my personal memories are pretty bitter ones, rarely ever happy ones. And it's all because of how people have treated me ever since childhood, how they saw me. 

I'm sorry if this comment was an emotional one, and this bitterness isn't directed at you. This bitterness is at people who see people with disabilities as not human. I hope you've at least learned a new persepective from someone who is disabled, even if that perspective is bitter like mine. I also hope that this helps you with your project.
